title: Tobin and the Lighthouse Secret
markdown:
The Sea-Spray Lighthouse stood white against a restless sea. Judging Day had come, and Tobin the goat felt his knees consider other careers. “Right, Felix. Inspector Sterling at ten. Everything must be perfect.” His spectacles made a break for the end of his nose.

Felix the stoat zipped past with an oil can. “The wind vane is sticking. It’s making a dreadful noise.”

Tobin waved a hoof. “Sea spray. Sterling expects competence, not complaints.” He puffed his chest in imitation of tavern captains he had admired from a safe distance.

Felix knew the truth was a loose bolt, and that a blind vane was a lighthouse lying about the weather. Tobin was already practising his speech on lamp calibration, hooves tapping a nervous tattoo.

Below, the market fried dough into the salt air. Tobin pictured Sterling’s eyes and tried not to.

Before ten he climbed to the gallery. For a minute he did nothing useful at all. He watched a fishing boat sew a white stitch across the water, and the tower hummed around him as if it had opinions it was too polite to shout. Then he remembered the performance, and the minute ended.

At ten-oh-three Inspector Sterling arrived. Her gaze swept the spotless lamp room. “Impressive upkeep, Keeper Tobin. Your predecessor, Heledd… she was… enthusiastic.”

Tobin beamed, missing the dry weather in the words. “Enthusiastic is my middle name.” He winced. His middle name was Reginald.

A gust slammed the tower. Glass rattled. Wood groaned. The vane screamed. Tobin froze. He had forgotten the north-facing storm shutter. A banging shutter could drown a foghorn. “The shutter. The vane.” His hooves tangled. The calm he had borrowed from captains went home without him.

Felix moved as if panic were a draft he declined to stand in. While Tobin flailed, the stoat opened a hidden panel, nudged a loose wire into its terminal, and woke a secondary beacon — a dimmer light, the sort fog prefers.

Sterling watched the goat’s scramble, then the stoat’s hands. Soft light pulsed. “Keeper Tobin. What is that secondary light?”

“I don’t know. It’s never done that before.” He glanced at Felix, who was grooming his whiskers as if the crisis had been a speck.

Sterling’s mouth considered a smile. She looked from the loud keeper to the quiet one. “It appears the true guardian of the Sea-Spray’s beam is not quite as vocal as the posting suggests.”

She crouched to Felix’s height. “This stoat hears the lighthouse. You, Keeper, have been shouting at it.” A beat. “The secondary light is for fog. And the vane — a bolt, I presume?”

Tobin’s ears drooped. “Yes. Felix tried to tell me this morning.”

Sterling’s report, when it came, was mild, with a commendation for unconventional problem-solving that made Tobin want to hide inside his own horns. She left them the sea and the hum.

Later Tobin sat by the lamp. The wind howled; the tower answered steadily. “Felix. I was so busy looking like a keeper.” He did not finish the confession with a moral. He held out the oil can.

Felix hopped onto his knee and nudged his chin. “We keep it running. Together.”

Tobin let the strained smile drop. The beam swept the darkening water, ordinary and sufficient, and for once he did not narrate it.
characters: Tobin (a goat lighthouse helper), Felix (a stoat lab partner)
